title: Ampesi
localName: Ampesi — boiled plantain, yam or cocoyam
author: Afua Boateng
desc: Plantains boiled in their skins fifteen to twenty minutes until fork-tender — half of the Akan pairing whose other half is kontomire stew.
longDesc: Ampesi is boiled starch, and its simplicity is the point: plantain, yam or cocoyam, cooked in plenty of salted water until fork-tender and served with a stew poured beside rather than over it. Four large unpeeled plantains, fifteen to twenty minutes, fork-tender. It is one half of a fixed Akan pairing — the other half is kontomire stew, and one named Ghanaian author describes kontomire stew as one of the two components of an Akan classic, which is ampesi. Only the plantain timing is documented; yam and cocoyam times are not published anywhere consulted.
ingredients: Yam, peeled and cut into rounds
steps: Wash the plantains and trim the ends, leaving the skins on.
Cut into large sections if the pot is small.
Cover with water, salt it, and bring to the boil.
Drain, and peel while still warm.
Serve alongside kontomire stew (GHA023) or garden egg stew, with the stew beside the starch rather than poured over it.
chefTips: Skins on while boiling. They hold the plantain together and slip off easily once it is cooked.
Fork-tender, not soft. Ampesi is meant to hold its shape on the plate — this is not fufu and it is not mashed.
Fifteen to twenty minutes is for plantain. Yam and cocoyam take longer, and no source consulted publishes their times, so test with a fork rather than trusting a number.
Salt the water generously. It is the only seasoning the starch gets.
Peel while warm. Cold plantain skin clings.
The pairing with kontomire stew is not a suggestion but the standard form — an Akan cook describes the two as the components of one classic dish.
Half-ripe plantain gives the best ampesi: firm enough to hold, sweet enough to taste of something.
commonMistakes: Peeling before boiling, which lets the plantain waterlog.
Boiling until soft, so it breaks up.
Using a yam or cocoyam time borrowed from the plantain figure.
Pouring the stew over the top rather than serving it beside.
sources: Plantain quantities and timing from 'Ampesi (Boiled Plantains)', in the Africa News Cookbook material as compiled in 'Recipes from Ghana', credited on the page to 'From Carol Miller-Tutzauer, University at Buffalo', dated Fri 13 Sept 1991, hosted at africa.upenn.edu. As printed: 4 large unpeeled plantains; cook 15-20 minutes 'until fork-tender'. ATTRIBUTION FLAG: the credit for this specific entry is not explicit on the page, which credits several published cookbooks collectively; the compilation is cited rather than an individual author.

THE PAIRING, from Afia Amoako writing as Eat with Afia, verbatim: 'Kontomire stew is one of the two components of an Akan classic: Ampesi.' This is the source for treating the two as one dish rather than a starch with an optional sauce.

GAP, named rather than filled: NO acceptable standalone ampesi source with YAM or COCOYAM cooking times was found. The 15-to-20-minute window above is for plantain only. The alternatives are listed in the ingredients without times because no source publishes them.

A SOURCE CHECKED AND PARTLY SET ASIDE: 'Nadia's Ampesi With Kontomire Stew', fromourplace.ca, creator credit as printed 'Nadia Ampesi (@travelndmunchies)', yield 4-5 servings. FLAGS: the host is a cookware brand's blog and the creator credit is a social handle. Its kontomire component is quantified in full and is used at GHA023, but its page gives NO cooking times for the starch, which is the ampesi part — so it contributes nothing to this entry. Its stew is also an adaptation, using spinach, smoked paprika and dried parsley, and is labelled as such where it appears.
NO SENSORY CUE beyond 'fork-tender' is published for this dish. The guidance about half-ripe plantain in the tips is general cooking practice and is NOT asserted as sourced.

ON SERVING: that the stew goes beside the starch rather than over it is standard Ghanaian practice and is how the paired sources present the dish; no source states it as an instruction, so it is offered as practice rather than quoted.
reheating: Steam, or pan-fry the slices in a little oil.
healthBenefits: Plantain is high in potassium, vitamin A and vitamin B6.
Half-ripe plantain carries substantial resistant starch, which has a lower glycaemic impact.
culturalNote: Ampesi and kontomire stew are treated as one dish rather than two by Akan cooks, which is why a recipe for either on its own looks incomplete. It is weekday food — quick, cheap, no pounding — and the plate is assembled with the boiled starch on one side, the dark green stew on the other, and often a boiled egg and sliced avocado alongside.
